title: Why XOR needs a second layer
objectives: Show that no single neuron computes XOR, and build it from two layers of neurons.

screens.title: Exactly one
screens.prose: **XOR** fires when exactly one input is 1: on $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$, not on $(0, 0)$ or $(1, 1)$. Try to set one neuron that does it.
screens.question: Could you make $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ fire, and neither of the other two?

options.text: No: whatever I set, a wrong corner fires or a right one does not
Yes, with large enough weights on both inputs
options.why: Large weights move the same straight line. Check the caption: $(1, 1)$ or $(0, 0)$ always joins in, or a corner drops out.

options.text: Yes, with a bias of exactly 0 and equal weights
options.why: With bias 0, $(0, 0)$ sits on the line and does not fire, but then $(1, 1)$ fires whenever the single corners do.

hints.text: To fire on $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ but not $(1, 1)$, which way must the line cut?
One straight line cannot put the two diagonal corners on one side and the other two on the other.

feedback.correct: No line does it: the corners that should fire sit on a diagonal.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep trying settings and read the caption.

explain.text: The two corners that should fire lie on one diagonal, the two that should not on the other. A single straight line cannot separate them. The next screen proves it.

screens.title: Why no neuron can
screens.prose: Suppose one neuron, weights $w_1$, $w_2$ and bias $b$, did compute XOR. Follow what that would force.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Add those two, since true inequalities that point the same way can be added: $w_1 + w_2 + 2b > 0$
Take $b$ from both sides: $w_1 + w_2 + b > -b$
From the first line, $-b \ge 0$, so $w_1 + w_2 + b > 0$
So $(1, 1)$ fires, which XOR forbids: no single neuron computes XOR
Multiply the two inequalities: $(w_1 + b)(w_2 + b) > 0$

hints.text: Write what each corner forces first.
Two inequalities that point the same way can be added.
Corners, add, rearrange, use $b \le 0$, conclude.

feedback.correct: Three corners force $(1, 1)$ to fire: a contradiction.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each line must follow from earlier ones.

byKey.x1: Multiplying gives nothing about $w_1 + w_2 + b$. Adding is the step that works.
byKey.d6: That line needs both $b \le 0$ and the rearranged sum first.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the multiplication belongs.

explain.text: The three corners give $b \le 0$, $w_1 + b > 0$ and $w_2 + b > 0$. Adding the last two and using $-b \ge 0$ gives $w_1 + w_2 + b > 0$. So $(1, 1)$ fires whatever the numbers: no single neuron computes XOR.

screens.title: Two layers
screens.prose: Feed the inputs to two neurons, OR (2, 2, −1) and NAND (−2, −2, 3). A third neuron, AND (2, 2, −3), takes their two outputs as its inputs.

state.caption: Solid edges carry a positive weight, dashed edges a negative one.

screens.question: Fill in each neuron's output.

hints.text: Fill the OR and NAND columns first, then AND of those two.
At $(1, 1)$: OR is 1, NAND is 0.
Outputs 0, 1, 1, 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. AND fires only when both OR and NAND are 1.

explain.text: OR is 0, 1, 1, 1 and NAND is 1, 1, 1, 0. Both are 1 only for $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$, so AND gives 0, 1, 1, 0: XOR.

screens.title: Counting the numbers
screens.prose: Each neuron has a weight for each input and one bias. These are the **numbers the network learns**; `stat-learning` l17 will call them parameters.

state.caption: Solid edges carry a positive weight, dashed edges a negative one.

screens.question: How many numbers does the two-layer XOR network have?

hints.text: First layer: two neurons, each with 2 weights and a bias.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count weights and biases in both layers.

byKey.weights: 6 counts the weights only. Add the three biases.

explain.text: The first layer has 4 weights and 2 biases; the output neuron has 2 weights and 1 bias. That is $4 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9$.

screens.title: A bigger neuron?
screens.prose: A classmate says: “One neuron with weights of 100 would manage XOR.”
screens.question: What is wrong with that?

options.text: One neuron draws one line at any size; the proof covers all numbers
Nothing: big enough weights would make it work
options.why: The proof used no sizes at all. It rules out every weight and bias.

options.text: The weights should be small and careful instead
options.why: Size does not matter: one neuron draws one line either way.

hints.text: Did the proof assume anything about how big the weights are?
No: it holds for every $w_1$, $w_2$ and $b$.

feedback.correct: Size changes nothing: one neuron, one line.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look back at the proof.

byKey.right: You trusted size. The proof shows $(1, 1)$ must fire for any weights.

explain.text: The proof never used the sizes of the numbers. Weights of 100 just move or tilt the same single line. XOR needs a second layer.

screens.title: Checking by search
screens.prose: A program tries every weight and bias from −5 to 5 in steps of 0.5. It finds no single neuron that computes XOR.
screens.question: How many neurons does the search try?

hints.text: How many values from −5 to 5 in steps of 0.5?
21 values for each of the three numbers.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the values for one number, then multiply.

byKey.per: 21 is for one number. There are three: $w_1$, $w_2$ and $b$.
byKey.ten: There are 21 values, not 11: steps of 0.5.
byKey.one-short: From −5 to 5 in steps of 0.5 is 21 values, not 20.

explain.text: Each number takes 21 values, so the search tries $21^3 = 9261$ neurons and none works. A search only covers the values it tries; the proof covers every number.

screens.title: XOR in code
screens.prose: `fires(weights, inputs, bias)` is ready for you to call.
screens.question: Write `xor_net(x1, x2)` from three calls to `fires`: OR, NAND, then AND of their outputs.

widget.starter:
def xor_net(x1, x2):
    # first layer: an OR neuron and a NAND neuron
    # second layer: an AND neuron on their two outputs
    return 0
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests: all four inputs, and that your code calls `fires` at least three times.

hints.text: `h1 = fires([2, 2], [x1, x2], -1)` is the OR neuron.
`return fires([2, 2], [h1, h2], -3)`.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: Build the network from `fires` calls, not with `!=` or `^`: three calls in all.
byKey.test-4: At (1, 1) NAND is 0, so AND must give 0.

explain.text:
The first layer turns the inputs into OR and NAND; the second takes AND of those.

```python
h1 = fires([2, 2], [x1, x2], -1)
h2 = fires([-2, -2], [x1, x2], 3)
return fires([2, 2], [h1, h2], -3)
```

screens.title: Layers draw shapes
screens.prose: One neuron draws one line. A second layer combines lines: here two lines fence off the diagonal corners. $$\text{XOR} = \text{AND}(\text{OR},\ \text{NAND})$$ Many layers is the “deep” in deep learning.
screens.question: Each first-layer neuron draws one line. How many lines fence off XOR's two corners here?

hints.text: Count the first-layer neurons.
OR and NAND: two lines.

feedback.correct: Two lines, one from OR and one from NAND.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the neurons in the first layer.

byKey.three: The AND neuron draws no line on the corners; it combines the two lines.

explain.text: OR cuts off $(0, 0)$ and NAND cuts off $(1, 1)$: 2 lines. The corners between them are XOR's, and AND picks them out.

screens.title: Exactly one strong signal
screens.prose: A researcher's signal is good only when exactly one of momentum and value is strong: both strong usually means a crowded trade.
screens.question: Can a single threshold rule on the two (strong = 1, weak = 0) express this?

options.text: No: it is XOR, so it needs two layers

options.why: This is XOR. The proof rules out every single neuron.
AND fires when both are strong, exactly the case to avoid.

hints.text: Write the four cases: which ones are good?
(1, 0) and (0, 1): exactly one, which is XOR.

feedback.correct: It is XOR: one threshold rule cannot do it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List when the signal is good.

explain.text: Good on (1, 0) and (0, 1), bad on (0, 0) and (1, 1): that is XOR. A one-neuron rule draws one line and cannot express it; a two-layer rule can.

ideas: XOR fires when exactly one input is 1; no single neuron computes it, for any weights and bias.
Proof: the three corners force $w_1 + w_2 + b > 0$, so $(1, 1)$ would fire.
Two layers do it: AND of OR and NAND, with 9 numbers to learn.
summary.trap: Bigger weights do not help: one neuron always draws one straight line.

quiz.question: For how many of the four inputs does XOR give 1?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Exactly one input must be 1.

explain.text: XOR fires when exactly one input is 1: 2 of the four inputs.

quiz.prose: A network has 2 inputs, a first layer of 3 neurons, and 1 output neuron.
quiz.question: How many numbers does it learn?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count weights and biases in both layers.

byKey.no-bias: Count a bias for each of the 4 neurons.

explain.text: First layer: 3 neurons with 2 weights and a bias each, 9 numbers. Output: 3 weights and a bias, 4. Total 13.

quiz.question: Why does XOR need a second layer?

options.text: One neuron draws one straight line, and no line separates XOR's corners
XOR needs bigger weights than any one neuron allows
options.why: Weights can be any size; the trouble is the single line.

options.text: XOR has three inputs, one more than a neuron takes
options.why: XOR here has two inputs, and a neuron can take any number.

feedback.correct: One line cannot split the diagonal corners.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about the picture.

explain.text: XOR's yes corners lie on one diagonal and its no corners on the other. No single line splits them, so a second layer combines two lines.
